strengths: Provides first analytically tractable model for inference-time scaling using Bayesian regression and deterministic equivalents, a novel theoretical framework for this practically important problem

Derives multiple complementary insights with rigorous mathematics: optimal reward differs from teacher (Remark 2), finite optimal k exists under misspecification (Remark 3), optimal temperature exists (Remark 4), and best-of-k scales as Θ(1/k²) with explicit constants
Sophisticated technical analysis combining high-dimensional RMT, controlled cumulant expansions, and extreme value theory with careful attention to domain conditions and rigorous proofs
Validates key predictions qualitatively on real LLMs (Llama-3-8B + Mistral-7B on GSM8K), including novel prediction of optimal sampling temperature for reward process
Clear presentation of main results with good intuition; effective figures (Figures 2-6) showing theory-experiment agreement in synthetic setting
weaknesses: Critical model-practice gap: Core analysis assumes linear teacher y = wT·x/√d with quadratic reward, but real LLMs are highly nonlinear. Claims about 'demystifying LLM-as-a-judge' are overstated given these restrictive assumptions. Unclear why insights should transfer to neural networks with billions of parameters

Synthetic experiments use small dimensions (d=10 to d=101) despite theory requiring d→∞, and Figure 10 shows results qualitatively change for d≥n. LLM experiments show high variance (Figure 7-8 with ~10% noise) and are qualitative only with no quantitative fit to theory

Restrictive and often-unverified domain conditions: Result 1 requires σ ≪ σc(α,R); Result 2 requires T ≫ s(x)²; Result 3 requires ordered limits T→0 then k→∞; Remark 2 requires perturbative regime (Eq. 19); Remark 6 requires R ≪ σ² and other constraints. Applicability unclear and conditions rarely verified in experiments

Limited practical actionability: Optimal formulas (e.g., Remark 2, 4) require knowing model internals (BR, m(x), s(x)², C1, C2) that depend on linear structure and cannot be computed for real LLMs. Unclear how practitioners would use results without full model knowledge

Insufficient experimental validation: Only GSM8K tested (math problems); need diverse tasks. Single generation with deterministic judge limits statistical power. How is correctness defined? Robustness to label noise? Missing error bars and seed information in Figures 7-8

Incomplete analysis: Boundary behavior between regions R and R^c not characterized. Connection between task difficulty and inference advantage (abstract claim) only briefly mentioned in Remark 5. Limited substantive comparison with related work (Levi 2024, Chen et al. 2024a). Task difficulty dependence unexplored

Reproducibility concerns: GitHub link referenced but URL not provided. LLM experiment prompts only partially specified ('simple/weak' vs 'detailed/strong'). Chain-of-thought demonstrations not detailed. Number of seeds and error propagation methods not specified

Technical limitations: Remark 2's formula valid only under assumption (19) not experimentally verified. Error bounds for Result 2's series expansion (O(t⁻⁴)) not provided. How tight is the approximation for moderate t? Sensitivity analysis missing for key choices (prior scale γ, reward function form)

strengths: Novel unified theoretical framework using Bayesian linear regression with deterministic equivalents that provides closed-form analysis of inference-time scaling
Comprehensive theoretical analysis across complementary regimes: high-T expansion, low-T best-of-k, optimal temperature, and training-inference trade-offs
Novel predictions that optimal reward differs from teacher model and optimal temperature exists for reward sampling, validated empirically
Technically rigorous proofs using random matrix theory; deterministic equivalents derivation appears sound
Serious attempt at experimental validation on both simplified linear model and real LLMs (multiple models on GSM8K)
Clear presentation with excellent visualizations showing phase transitions and optimal values
Addresses important practical problem of inference-time compute allocation
weaknesses: Large theory-practice gap: linear regression with quadratic reward fundamentally different from nonlinear LLM behavior with complex reward structures; generalization not fully justified beyond empirical observation
Restrictive quadratic reward assumption r(y,x) = -(y - wR·x/√d)²; real process reward models can have nonmonotonic structure; robustness to other reward forms unexplored
Key small noise assumption σ ≪ σc(α,R) in Result 1 not thoroughly validated; σc not explicitly computed; theory may break down with larger noise

Empirical LLM validation has significant gaps: error metric (Eq. 27) differs from theory without clear justification; high variance in some results (Figure 9); connection between theoretical parameters and actual judge alignment not established; limited to one domain (GSM8K)
Restrictive parameter regimes for main conclusions: trade-off analysis (Remark 6) requires T→0, k→∞, and specific conditions on ridge and regularization that may not hold generally
Limited novelty in some aspects: deterministic equivalents technique is established; best-of-k scaling explored before (Brown et al. 2024, Schaeffer et al. 2025b); optimal temperature is more novel
Best-of-k analysis (Result 3) assumes perfect reward wR = wT; minimal analysis of misspecified rewards limits applicability
Code availability status unclear (placeholder link); reproducibility concerns until code released
Experimental design choices not justified (temperature 0.2, 8 exemplars, weak/strong prompts); no ablation studies; generalization to other domains unknown

strengths: Technically sound theoretical analysis using deterministic equivalents with rigorous proofs in appendices
Multiple analytical regimes studied (high-T expansion, low-T best-of-k limit) providing complementary perspectives
Some interesting observations: optimal reward differs from teacher, existence of optimal sampling temperature
Comprehensive presentation with extensive appendices, edge case discussions (beam search, self-consistency), and detailed experimental protocols
weaknesses: Severe model-reality gap: core model assumes Bayesian linear regression with Gaussian inputs and quadratic rewards, while LLMs are nonlinear with discrete outputs and complex reward structure. Section 4 only provides qualitative agreement without quantitative predictions.

Weak empirical validation: experiments mostly confirm phenomena already known from prior work (Snell et al. 2025, Du et al. 2025). No quantitative testing of theoretical predictions (e.g., Remark 4 formula for optimal T, Remark 5 scaling coefficients). Single dataset (GSM8K validation).

Limited novelty: optimal k under imperfect rewards is intuitive, reward quality mattering is obvious, optimal T follows from bias-variance tradeoff, best-of-k Θ(1/k²) is unsurprising and only proven for perfect reward case

Restrictive regime conditions: underparameterized regime (d/n < 1) contradicts modern overparameterized LLMs; requirement σ ≪ σc(α,R) poorly characterized; optimal reward formula (Remark 2) valid only when reward already aligned; best-of-k result requires perfect reward

Gap in key results: Remark 2 applies where misalignment is small; Result 3 avoids misspecified reward case; Remark 6 requires exact teacher access and very specific conditions; Figure 12 shows empirical k^−α with α ≠ 2, contradicting theory

Incomplete practical bridge: unclear how to estimate wT, wR, σ from LLMs; generalization error definition (Eq. 27) for LLMs is ad-hoc and disconnected from theory; no actionable guidance for practitioners

Missing quantitative validation: no experiments testing theoretical predictions numerically on LLMs, no ablations on reward quality showing monotonicity threshold, no sensitivity analysis, limited scope to single task

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in LLM inference scaling with the first rigorous analytical framework
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with multiple complementary perspectives (deterministic equivalents, high-T expansion, extreme value theory)
Novel insights including optimal reward differing from teacher, existence of optimal k under misspecification, and optimal temperature for reward selection
Strong experimental validation on toy model with perfect theory-experiment agreement (Figure 2)
Empirical validation on real LLMs reveals new phenomena (optimal T) supporting theoretical predictions
Mathematically sound with rigorous proofs and correct application of advanced techniques (deterministic equivalents, extreme value theory)
Clear presentation with well-organized progression from theory to experiments
weaknesses: Significant gap between theoretical model (linear, quadratic reward, Gaussian inputs) and practical LLMs (nonlinear, learned rewards, discrete tokens)
Incomplete quantitative validation on LLMs - Figure 12 notes exponent of k differs from theoretical k^(-2) prediction, indicating theory may not fully capture LLM behavior
Limited practical applicability - formulas for optimal T and reward require unknown quantities (m(x), s(x), BR) with no guidance for estimation
Results mostly confirm empirically known phenomena rather than providing surprising new insights
Restrictive and hard-to-verify assumptions: Result 1 requires σ ≪ σ_c(α,R) with poorly characterized threshold; independence assumption violated in practice
High variance in some LLM experiments (Figs 8-9) and evaluation limited to single task (GSM8K) and domain (math)
Trade-off analysis (Remark 6) applies only to specific parameter regimes with limited real-world relevance
Inconsistency between theoretical generalization error (squared error, Eq. 8) and LLM metric (accuracy, Eq. 27) makes direct mapping unclear
